title: Microbes and microscopy
specPoints: Year 9 bridging: microbes, microscopes and the four groups of micro-organism

tips.title: Four groups, and only three are cells
tips.body: Bacteria, fungi and protists are **cells**: they feed, grow and divide on their own. A **virus** is genetic material in a protein coat and does none of that alone. Nearly every hard question in this topic turns on that line: what antibiotics can kill, what counts as alive, and what a microscope can show.

tips.title: Divisions first, then 2 to that power
tips.body: For a doubling question, count the **divisions** (minutes ÷ 20), then work out $2^n$. Nine divisions is $2^9 = 512$, not $9 \times 2 = 18$. If your answer after a few hours is in the tens, you have multiplied instead of doubling.

tips.title: Total magnification just multiplies
tips.body: Eyepiece × objective, every time. A ×10 eyepiece makes every objective ten times bigger: ×4 gives ×40, ×10 gives ×100, ×40 gives ×400. Write the **total** under a drawing, never the objective alone.

tips.title: Cold slows, heat kills
tips.body: A question about a fridge wants **slows the reactions of the bacteria**; a question about cooking or pasteurising wants **kills them**. Saying a fridge kills bacteria is the commonest lost mark in this topic, and it is wrong: the milk still goes off, only later.

tips.title: Why school plates sit at 25 °C
tips.body: Human pathogens grow best at body temperature, **37 °C**. Keeping the dish at **25 °C** lets harmless bacteria grow enough to see while making a dangerous one much less likely. Give the reason, not just the number.

why.matters: Most of the living things on Earth are too small to see, and nearly everything that happens to food, soil and bodies is done by them. Bread rises, milk turns to yoghurt, leaves rot into soil and a cold spreads round a class, all because of microbes, and none of it is visible without a lens. This topic is the picture behind the GCSE units that follow: which pathogens cause which diseases, how the immune system fights them, why antibiotics are failing, and why a fridge is a better friend than a bin. It starts by being able to say what a microbe is, which group it belongs to, and how fast it can multiply.

examples.title: A loaf of bread
examples.body: Every loaf is a microbe at work. Yeast, a single-celled fungus, is mixed into flour and water and left somewhere warm. It respires on the sugar in the flour and gives off carbon dioxide, which is trapped as bubbles and pushes the dough up. In the oven the heat kills the yeast and sets the dough round the bubbles, which is why a slice is full of holes. Put the dough in a cold room and it rises so slowly you would think the yeast had died: it has not, its reactions have just slowed down.

nodes.no: no: wait, or find somewhere warmer

visual.alt: A flow chart of bread making: yeast respires in warm dough, carbon dioxide bubbles make it rise, and once it has doubled the oven kills the yeast and sets the loaf

examples.title: The chicken on the counter
examples.body: One bacterium on a piece of chicken is nothing. Left on a warm counter it divides about every 20 minutes, and doubling runs away: 8 after an hour, 64 after two, 512 after three, over four thousand after four. By evening the count is in the millions, and that is a dose that makes you ill. Nothing about the chicken looks or smells different for most of that time. A fridge does not kill the bacteria, it stretches each doubling from minutes to hours, which is exactly what the use-by date is counting.

visual.alt: A table of bacteria grown from one cell on a warm counter: one, eight, sixty-four, five hundred and twelve and four thousand and ninety-six after zero to four hours

examples.title: A drop of pond water
examples.body: In the 1670s a Dutch cloth merchant, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, ground a lens good enough to look at a drop of pond water and found it full of swimming creatures nobody had known existed. That single lens opened the whole subject. The sizes are the surprise: a cheek cell is about 20 micrometres across, a bacterium a tenth of that, and a virus so much smaller again that no light microscope can show one at all, however hard you magnify. Seeing more needed a different kind of microscope, which is where the GCSE picks the story up.

steps.title: What a microbe is
steps.body:
A **microbe**, or micro-organism, is a living thing **too small to see without a microscope**. Most are a **single cell**. They are everywhere: in soil, in water, in the air, on your skin, and in enormous numbers inside your gut.

**How small is small?** Your cheek cells are about **20 µm** across (a micrometre, µm, is a thousandth of a millimetre). A **bacterium** is about **2 µm** long, so ten of them would fit across one of your cells. A **virus** is about **100 nm** (nanometres, a thousandth of a micrometre), so twenty of them would fit across one bacterium. The bars in the picture are drawn to true scale, and the virus bar is a single pixel.

**Why nobody knew.** Microbes were invisible until the microscope. In the **1670s** Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth merchant who ground his own lenses, looked at a drop of pond water and saw it swarming with what he called *animalcules*: the first microbes anyone had seen. Every idea in this unit, from why food goes off to why you get ill, was impossible before that moment.

**Two things to hold on to.** Most microbes are **harmless or useful**; the few that cause disease are called **pathogens**. And because they are so small, they are counted in **millions**, which is why they can change things so fast.

check.prompt: A cheek cell is about 20 µm across and a bacterium about 2 µm long. How many bacteria would fit end to end across the cell?
check.solution: $20 \div 2 = 10$. **Ten** bacteria fit across one cheek cell, which is why a single cell can carry so many of them.

steps.title: The four groups
steps.body:
Microbes are sorted into **four groups**, and the first question about any microbe is *which group?*, because the group decides what it can do and how it can be stopped.

- **Bacteria** are single cells with **no nucleus**; their DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm. Most are harmless. Some cause disease, often by releasing **toxins**. Examples: the bacteria that make yoghurt, and *Salmonella* in badly cooked chicken.
- **Fungi** are cells **with a nucleus**. **Yeast** is a single cell; **moulds** grow as threads through bread or fruit. They feed on what they grow on.
- **Protists** are single cells **with a nucleus** that live in water or in other organisms. **Amoeba** in a pond; the protist that causes **malaria** in blood.
- **Viruses** are **not cells at all**: a strand of genetic material inside a **protein coat**, far smaller than any cell. A virus cannot feed, grow or divide by itself. It gets inside a living cell and makes the cell build copies, which usually kills the cell. Colds, flu, measles and chickenpox are all viruses.

**The line that matters most is the last one.** Bacteria, fungi and protists are alive in the ordinary sense: cells that feed, grow and divide. A virus does none of that on its own, and this is why the medicines that kill bacteria do nothing to a virus, which you meet in the next topic.

check.prompt: Which group of microbes is not made of cells?
check.solution: **Viruses.** A virus is genetic material in a protein coat, with no cytoplasm, no membrane and no way to feed or divide on its own. The other three groups are all living cells.

steps.title: Useful microbes
steps.body:
Most of what microbes do is useful, and some of it we depend on.

**Bread.** Yeast is mixed into dough and left somewhere warm. It **respires**, using the sugar in the flour and releasing **carbon dioxide**. The gas is trapped as bubbles, so the dough **rises**. In the oven the heat **kills the yeast** and sets the bread, and the holes in a slice are where the bubbles were.

**Yoghurt and cheese.** Bacteria added to warm milk feed on the milk sugar (lactose) and turn it into **lactic acid**. The acid makes the milk protein thicken and gives yoghurt its sharp taste. Cheese starts the same way.

**Decomposers.** Bacteria and fungi in the soil **break down dead plants and animals** and waste, releasing the **nutrients** back into the soil so plants can use them again. Without decomposers, nothing would rot and the nutrients would stay locked in the dead material. This is also what a compost heap is doing.

**Your gut.** Trillions of bacteria live in your intestines. They help **digest fibre** you could not digest alone, make some **vitamins**, and take up the space that harmful bacteria would otherwise use.

**Medicines.** Some antibiotics come from fungi, and bacteria with a human gene added make the **insulin** that people with diabetes inject. Both come back later in the course.

steps.title: Harmful microbes, and how they spread
steps.body:
A microbe that causes disease is a **pathogen**. Each of the four groups has some.

- **Bacteria** multiply in the body and many release **toxins** that damage tissue: food poisoning, tuberculosis, tooth decay.
- **Viruses** get inside cells and **burst** them as copies are released: colds, flu, measles, chickenpox.
- **Fungi** grow into skin or tissue and feed on it: athlete's foot, ringworm.
- **Protists** live inside the body and destroy cells: malaria, spread by mosquitoes.

**How they get from one person to the next.** A pathogen has to travel, and each route has a way of blocking it.

- Through the **air**, in droplets from a cough or sneeze: cover your mouth, open windows.
- In **water** and **food**: clean water, cooking food properly, washing hands before eating.
- By **touch**, directly or from surfaces: hand washing, cleaning surfaces.
- Through **animals** that carry it, such as the mosquito carrying malaria: nets, insect repellent.
- Through **body fluids**, such as blood: sterile needles, condoms.

The practical point is that **hand washing** blocks more of these routes than anything else, which is why hospitals are so strict about it.

visuals.alt: A table of the routes a pathogen can take between people, a disease that uses each route, and what blocks it

check.prompt: Which of these blocks the spread of a pathogen carried in the droplets from a sneeze?
check.solution: Droplets travel through the **air**, so the block is to stop them leaving: cover the sneeze. Cooking, nets and sterile needles block the food, animal and body-fluid routes.

steps.title: How fast bacteria multiply
steps.body:
A bacterium reproduces by **splitting in two**, and in warm, moist conditions with food, some kinds do it about **every 20 minutes**. That is **3 divisions an hour**, and each division **doubles** the number.

Doubling is deceptive because it starts slowly. One bacterium becomes 2, then 4, then 8: after an hour there are only **8**. But after three hours there are **512**, after four hours **4096**, and after eight hours over **16 million**. A single bacterium on a chicken left out on a warm counter is a food-poisoning dose by the evening.

**The method:** count the divisions, then work out 2 to that power.

**Why fridges and ovens work.** Cold does not kill bacteria; it **slows their reactions**, so the doublings come hours apart instead of minutes. That is why food in a fridge lasts days rather than forever. **Heat** from cooking does kill them, which is why cooked food is safe and why milk is heated (pasteurised) before it is sold.

**Growing them on purpose.** In a lab, bacteria are grown on **agar jelly** in a dish. In school the dishes are kept at **25 °C**, not at body temperature, **37 °C**: the pathogens that live in people grow best at 37 °C, so keeping the dish cooler makes it far less likely that a dangerous one grows.

steps.title: The light microscope
steps.body:
A school microscope has a handful of parts, and each has one job.

- The **eyepiece lens** you look through, usually **×10**.
- The **objective lenses** on the turret above the specimen, usually **×4, ×10 and ×40**.
- The **stage**, with clips to hold the slide.
- The **light** or mirror beneath the stage, shining up through the specimen.
- The **coarse focus** knob, which moves the stage a long way, and the **fine focus**, which moves it a little.

**Total magnification multiplies.** The eyepiece magnifies the image the objective made, so the total is eyepiece **×** objective. A ×10 eyepiece with the ×40 objective gives **×400**. With the ×4 objective it gives ×40.

**Using it.** Start with the **lowest-power** objective, because it shows the widest area and the specimen is easiest to find. Focus with the **coarse** knob, then sharpen with the **fine** knob. Only then turn to a higher-power objective, and use the fine focus alone: the coarse knob at high power can drive the lens into the slide.

**The slide.** The specimen must be **thin**, so light can pass through it, and is usually **stained** so that colourless parts show: iodine for onion cells, methylene blue for cheek cells. The GCSE core practical adds the detail.

**Drawing what you see.** Pencil, clean single lines, no shading, label lines drawn with a ruler that touch the part they name, and the magnification written underneath. Draw what is there, not what the textbook shows.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Are viruses alive?** It depends what *alive* means. A virus has genes and it reproduces, but only by hijacking a living cell; on its own it cannot feed, respire, grow or divide. Most biologists treat it as being on the border, and a good answer says *why* rather than picking a side. The consequence is practical: **antibiotics kill bacteria by attacking parts of a bacterial cell**, such as its cell wall, and a virus has no such parts. There is nothing for the drug to hit.

**Doubling is a power, not a multiple.** Nine divisions give $2^9 = 512$ bacteria, not $9 \times 2 = 18$. The number of bacteria after $n$ divisions is $2^n$, and the growth looks slow at first and then runs away. Food safety rules are written round this: the danger is not the first hour on the counter but the sixth.

**Cold slows, heat kills.** A fridge does not sterilise anything. It slows the chemical reactions inside the bacteria, so they divide every few hours instead of every 20 minutes. Cooking to a high enough temperature destroys them. Keep the two apart in an answer.

**Why 25 °C and not 37 °C.** Human pathogens are adapted to body temperature. A school dish kept at 25 °C grows harmless soil and skin bacteria well enough to see, while making it much less likely that a pathogen multiplies. The lower temperature is a safety choice, not a convenience.

**Magnifying is not the same as seeing more.** A light microscope cannot separate two points closer than about **200 nm**, however much it magnifies; below that you get a bigger blur. A typical virus is about 100 nm, so no light microscope can show one. That limit is called **resolution**, and it is why the electron microscope, which comes in the GCSE Key concepts unit, changed what biologists could know.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **microbe** is a living thing too small to see without a microscope; most are harmless or useful, and the ones that cause disease are **pathogens**.
- Sizes: an animal cell about **20 µm**, a bacterium about **2 µm**, a virus about **100 nm**.
- **Four groups**: bacteria (cells, no nucleus), fungi (cells with a nucleus; yeast and moulds), protists (single cells with a nucleus), viruses (**not cells**: genes in a protein coat, reproducing only inside a host cell).
- **Useful**: yeast makes **carbon dioxide** that raises bread; bacteria make **lactic acid** that turns milk to yoghurt; **decomposers** return nutrients to the soil; gut bacteria digest fibre and make vitamins.
- **Harmful**: bacteria release toxins, viruses burst cells, fungi grow into tissue, protists such as malaria destroy cells.
- Pathogens spread by **air, water and food, touch, animal carriers and body fluids**; hand washing blocks the most routes.
- Bacteria **double** by splitting, about every **20 minutes** in ideal conditions: after $n$ divisions there are $2^n$; 3 hours is 9 divisions and **512** bacteria.
- **Cold slows** bacteria; **heat kills** them. School agar plates are kept at **25 °C**, below the 37 °C human pathogens prefer.
- Total magnification = **eyepiece × objective**: ×10 with ×40 is **×400**. Start on low power, coarse focus then fine, fine focus only at high power.
- A light microscope resolves to about **200 nm**, so it cannot show a virus.

questions.prompt: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting from one bacterium, how many are there after 2 hours?

questions.prompt: Why is a specimen stained before it is viewed under a light microscope?
questions.solution: The nucleus and other parts are nearly transparent, so light passes straight through and nothing is seen. A stain such as iodine or methylene blue **colours** them so they stand out. Thinness comes from cutting, and magnification from the lenses.

questions.prompt: A drop of pond water contains a single cell with a nucleus that moves about by itself and feeds on smaller cells. Which group of microbe is it?
questions.solution: A single cell **with a nucleus**, living free in water, is a **protist**. A bacterium has no nucleus, a fungus does not swim about, and a virus is not a cell.

questions.prompt: What would happen in a wood if all the decomposers were removed?
questions.solution: Decomposers **break down** dead material and **release the nutrients** into the soil. Without them, nothing rots: the dead material stays whole, the nutrients stay locked in it, and the soil is starved.

questions.prompt: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes in ideal conditions. Starting from one bacterium, how many are there after 6 hours? Give a whole number.

questions.prompt: Milk kept in a fridge at 4 °C still goes off after about a week. Which statement best explains this?
questions.solution: A fridge **slows**, it does not kill or stop. The doublings that took 20 minutes on the counter take hours in the cold, so the numbers still climb, but over days instead of hours. Only heat kills the bacteria.

questions.prompt: Bread dough rises faster in a warm kitchen than in a cold one. Which explanation links this to what you know about enzymes?
questions.solution: The gas comes from **respiration**, a chain of reactions run by **enzymes**. Enzymes work faster as the temperature rises towards their optimum, so the yeast releases carbon dioxide faster and the dough rises sooner. Too hot, and the enzymes are destroyed: the oven kills the yeast.

questions.prompt: A microbe is found that has no nucleus and releases a toxin that damages the gut. Which group is it most likely to be, and why?
questions.solution: Two clues. **No nucleus** rules out fungi and protists, which have one, and **a toxin** is how many bacteria cause harm. A virus also has no nucleus, but a virus is not a cell at all and harms by bursting cells, not by releasing toxins.

questions.prompt: Some scientists say viruses are not alive. Which is the strongest reason?
questions.solution: The case rests on what a virus **cannot do alone**: no feeding, no growth, no respiration, no division. It only reproduces inside a living cell. Size, being made of protein and causing disease are all true of other things that are clearly alive or clearly not.

questions.prompt: A doctor refuses to prescribe antibiotics for a child with flu but prescribes them for a child with a bacterial ear infection. Compare bacteria and viruses, and use the comparison to explain both decisions.
questions.solution:
A **bacterium** is a living cell. It has a **cell wall**, a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a loop of DNA lying free in the cytoplasm with no nucleus round it. It feeds, respires and **divides by itself**, doubling every 20 minutes or so in good conditions, and many bacteria harm the body by releasing **toxins**. A **virus** is not a cell at all: a strand of genetic material inside a **protein coat**, about a tenth the size of a bacterium. It cannot feed, grow or divide on its own. It **gets inside a living cell** and makes that cell build copies of it, which are released when the cell bursts.

That difference decides both prescriptions. An **antibiotic** works by damaging a part of a bacterial cell that human cells do not have, such as the **cell wall**, so the bacteria die and the patient's own cells are untouched. The ear infection is bacterial, so the drug has something to act on and is prescribed. Flu is a **virus**. It has no cell wall, no cytoplasm and no machinery of its own; while it is inside the child's cells it is protected by them, and the antibiotic has **nothing to attack**. It cannot help, so it is not given.

There is a second reason for refusing. Every time bacteria in the body meet an antibiotic that is not needed, the few that happen to resist it survive and multiply, so **antibiotic resistance** spreads and the drug works less well for the people who do need it. The flu will be cleared by the child's immune system; the ear infection needs the drug. Both decisions follow from the same fact: antibiotics kill cells, and a virus is not one.

questions.prompt: A poster in a school canteen says "Microbes are dangerous." Evaluate this statement, using examples of useful and harmful microbes.
questions.solution:
The poster is right about **some** microbes. **Pathogens** are the microbes that cause disease, and every group has them. *Salmonella* is a **bacterium** that multiplies in badly cooked chicken and releases **toxins** that damage the gut. Flu and colds are **viruses**, which get inside cells and burst them as copies are released. Athlete's foot is a **fungus** growing into skin, and malaria is a **protist** carried by mosquitoes that destroys blood cells. In a canteen the bacterial ones matter most, because warm food left out lets bacteria **double every 20 minutes**, and hand washing and proper cooking are exactly what stop them.

But the poster is wrong as a **rule**. Most microbes are harmless, and many are useful in ways we depend on. **Yeast**, a fungus, respires in dough and releases the **carbon dioxide** that makes bread rise: the canteen's own bread was made by a microbe. **Bacteria** turn milk sugar into **lactic acid** to make yoghurt and cheese. **Decomposers** in the soil break down dead plants and animals and return the nutrients that grow next year's crops. Trillions of **gut bacteria** in every person in the canteen help digest fibre and make vitamins, and crowd out the harmful kinds. Some antibiotics come from fungi.

So the statement is true of a small minority and misleading about the rest. A fairer poster would say **some microbes cause disease**, and then say what actually protects people in a canteen: wash your hands, keep hot food hot and cold food cold, and cook chicken through. That message is accurate, and it is the one that stops anyone getting ill.

markScheme.description: as the criteria

criteria.text: Gives at least two harmful examples with the group and how it harms, such as Salmonella bacteria releasing toxins or a virus bursting cells.
Gives at least two useful examples with what they do, such as yeast releasing carbon dioxide in bread, bacteria making lactic acid in yoghurt, decomposers, or gut bacteria.
Points out that most microbes are harmless or useful and that only pathogens cause disease.
Reaches a judgement: the statement is true of some microbes and misleading as a rule, and proposes a fairer wording or a hygiene message instead.

examTechnique.body:
This topic is tested with short recall, one calculation and a few *why* questions, and the marks are lost in the words rather than the ideas. **Name the group** whenever you name a microbe: *yeast, a fungus*; *Salmonella, a bacterium*. **Give the reason** with every rule: not *keep plates at 25 °C* but *at 25 °C, because human pathogens grow best at 37 °C*.

The calculation is doubling, and the trap is arithmetic: count the divisions, then raise 2 to that power. For a microscope question, total magnification is eyepiece × objective, and the answer is written with a × sign. If a question mentions a virus and a medicine, the answer almost always turns on *a virus is not a cell*.
examinerErrors: Calling a virus a cell, or saying it has a nucleus. It is genetic material in a **protein coat**, and it reproduces only inside a host cell.
Multiplying instead of doubling: 9 divisions written as 9 × 2 rather than **2 to the power 9**.
Saying a fridge **kills** bacteria. It **slows** them; only heat kills.
Giving the objective lens alone as the magnification, instead of **eyepiece × objective**.
Stating 25 °C without the reason: human pathogens grow best at **37 °C**, body temperature.
Saying antibiotics kill viruses, or that they treat a cold.
Naming a microbe without its group, so that the follow-up question about how it harms or how it is treated cannot be answered.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer sorts before it explains. Shown an unfamiliar microbe it uses two clues, **is it a cell** and **does it have a nucleus**, to place it in a group, and then says how that group causes harm and what will stop it. It handles doubling as a power, writes $2^{18} = 262\,144$ without flinching, and can say why the danger from food on a counter is the sixth hour rather than the first. It keeps *cold slows* and *heat kills* apart, gives 25 °C its reason, and when a question mentions a virus and an antibiotic it answers with the structure of a virus rather than with the word *doesn't work*. Asked whether a virus is alive, it gives the case both ways and says which criterion decides it.
